title: Independent Events Cannot Be Mutually Exclusive
quickIdea: Mutually exclusive means P(A and B) = 0. Independent means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). If both events have positive probability, no pair can be both.
remember: Disjoint gives P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Independence gives P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). They answer different questions and are not two words for the same thing.
If P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0 and A, B are disjoint, then 0 = P(A and B) < P(A)P(B), so the pair is dependent - as dependent as a pair can be.
The only events that are both disjoint and independent have probability zero: P(A) = 0 or P(B) = 0 makes both sides 0.
Independent events of positive probability must overlap, so for them P(A or B) < P(A) + P(B).

Repeated tosses are independent because they are separate experiments. The outcomes of one toss are disjoint because they are one experiment. Mixing the two constructions is where the confusion starts.
NCERT's class 12 chapter states the lemma in this form: independent events with non-zero probability can never be mutually exclusive.

example.prompt: A fair die is rolled. A = an odd number, B = an even number. Are A and B independent, mutually exclusive, or both?
example.work: A and B cannot happen together, so P(A and B) = 0. But P(A) = 1/2 and P(B) = 1/2, so P(A)P(B) = 1/4. The product test fails, so the events are dependent; the disjointness is exactly what makes them dependent. Their union has probability 1 = 1/2 + 1/2, which is the disjoint addition rule at work.
example.answer: Mutually exclusive and dependent, with P(A or B) = 1.

gateAngle: An option of the form 'A and B are mutually exclusive and independent' is false in every GATE question that offers it, unless one of the probabilities is zero - and no CSE paper has yet offered that degenerate case.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Two events have P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3 and are disjoint. Are they independent?
variations.why: P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the product test fails. Disjointness of positive-probability events always means dependence.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.5, P(A and B) = 0.1. Are A and B independent? Are they mutually exclusive?
variations.why: P(A)P(B) = 0.15 is not 0.1, so they are dependent; P(A and B) = 0.1 is not 0, so they are not disjoint. This is the pair of verdicts GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.17 asks for.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Can two events with P(A) = 0 and P(B) = 0.7 be both disjoint and independent?
variations.answer: Yes, and this is the only way.
variations.why: P(A and B) = 0 because A is empty, and P(A)P(B) = 0 x 0.7 = 0, so both conditions hold. A zero-probability event is independent of everything.

trap.what: Reading 'independent' as 'unrelated' or 'cannot happen at the same time'.
trap.why: Independence is a statement that knowing one event leaves the other's probability unchanged. Disjointness is the strongest possible change: knowing one happened makes the other impossible.
trap.counterexample: Odd and even on a die are as disjoint as events get, and they are dependent for exactly that reason: P(odd|even) = 0 against P(odd) = 1/2.

check.question: P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3. Can A and B be both independent and mutually exclusive?
check.explanation: Independence would need P(A and B) = 0.06 while exclusivity needs P(A and B) = 0. Both cannot hold for positive probabilities.
